title: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition) · Units 21–22
description: Curated B2 vocabulary for music, digital audio, musical ability, flavours, food quality, restaurant dining and hosting.
sourceNotice: Prepared from the user-supplied book for personal study. Vocabulary targets follow source topics and selected exercises; all example sentences and teaching notes are newly written, and original exercises, extended passages and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Teaching sections, photographed instrument labels, footnotes, usage notes, exercises and relevant answer-key entries checked for lexical, grammatical and thematic coverage.
audit.pronunciation: Selected broad British IPA for checked words and concise expressions; longer expressions may omit IPA rather than present an unreliable transcription. Connected speech and regional variation are not exhaustively represented.
audit.languagePolicy: All content is in English except Brazilian Portuguese translations under pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Manual source-to-item and answer-key comparison; lexical, collocational, spelling, provenance and structural checks; word-target and example-audio text checks. Browser speech recognition and live app import were not tested.
audit.limitations: Empty audio fields indicate no bundled recordings. TTS and voice-recognition performance depend on browser and voice; no browser-based or live application import test was performed.

units.title: Unit 21 — Music
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 48–49 (PDF pages 49–50).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Describe downloading, synchronising, streaming and organising digital music.
Name typical rock-band roles, instruments and music genres accurately.
Discuss musical preferences and recognise natural expressions for musical ability.
Use fixed collocations with music and avoid treating the noun music as countable.

items.example: I copied the MP3 file to a folder on my laptop.
items.note: A compressed audio-file format; the unit uses it as a familiar music-download example.

items.example: The band's latest album contains twelve tracks.
items.note: A collection of recordings released together, physically or digitally.

items.example: The final track is longer than the others.
items.note: An individual song or piece within an album.

items.example: She created a playlist for her journey.
items.note: A selected collection of tracks played in an arranged or saved order.

items.example: He prefers to download music before travelling.
items.note: To copy audio to a device so it can be accessed locally; contrast with stream music.

items.example: My phone will sync with my laptop when I connect it.
items.note: Short, everyday form of synchronise; keep files or data aligned between devices.

items.example: The software can synchronise recordings across both devices.
items.note: More formal than sync; British spelling synchronise, American synchronize.

items.example: We usually stream music rather than store it offline.
items.note: To play audio received over a network as it is delivered.

items.example: She joined a rock band during her first year at university.
items.note: A group of musicians performing rock music.

items.example: The lead singer introduced the next song.
items.note: The main vocalist in a band.

items.example: She plays lead guitar and performs most of the solos.
items.note: The guitar part usually responsible for prominent melodies and solos.

items.example: The lead guitarist played an impressive solo.
items.note: The musician who plays the lead-guitar part.

items.example: Our keyboard is connected to a small amplifier.
items.note: A keyed instrument used in contemporary bands.

items.example: The keyboard player added strings to the arrangement.
items.note: A musician who plays electronic keyboards or similar instruments.

items.example: We could hear the drums from the rehearsal room.
items.note: A drum kit is usually played by a seated musician using sticks or pedals.

items.example: The drummer kept a steady beat throughout the concert.
items.note: A musician who plays the drums.

items.example: The bass gives the song a deep, warm sound.
items.note: For the instrument or low musical register, bass rhymes with face; do not confuse with the fish bass.

items.example: A skilled bass guitarist can make a simple song sound powerful.
items.note: A musician who plays bass guitar, usually contributing low notes.

items.example: She practises the guitar every evening.
items.note: The word guitar can refer to acoustic or electric instruments; Portuguese distinguishes violão and guitarra.

items.example: He learnt to play an instrument when he was eight.
items.note: Use play with the name of an instrument: play the drums or play the guitar.

items.example: Their tastes in music are completely different.
items.note: Taste in is the normal preposition for musical preferences.

items.example: She often listens to classical music while reading.
items.note: Say classical music, not classic music; music is uncountable.

items.example: The festival features folk music from several regions.
items.note: Music based on the traditions of a community or culture.

items.example: My grandfather is a folk fan who enjoys local festivals.
items.note: A fan of folk music; fan commonly combines with a genre or performer.

items.example: The café hosts a jazz performance on Thursdays.
items.note: A genre associated with improvisation and characteristic rhythms.

items.example: Her playlist combines jazz, pop and R&B.
items.note: Short for rhythm and blues; the term covers related and evolving styles.

items.example: Hip-hop became her favourite genre at university.
items.note: A music and cultural style often featuring rhythmic spoken vocals.

items.example: He started writing rap before he learnt to play an instrument.
items.note: Rhythmic spoken words in music; rap can also be a verb.

items.example: They compose music for independent films.
items.note: To create a piece of music; the noun is composition.

items.pt: curtir música; gostar muito de música
items.example: My cousin is really into music from the sixties.
items.note: Informal be into something means to be very interested in it.

items.example: The programme focuses on 60s music and popular culture.
items.note: The decade is the 1960s; 60s is a common shortened written form.

items.example: The film soundtrack includes several original songs.
items.note: Recorded music associated with a film; soundtracks can contain songs and instrumental pieces.

items.example: The shop played canned music all afternoon.
items.note: Often mildly negative or old-fashioned for recorded background music in public places.

items.example: I can't stand music played at full volume.
items.note: A strong informal way of saying you really dislike something; often followed by a noun or -ing form.

items.example: That tune is so repetitive that it drives me crazy.
items.note: Informal expression for making someone extremely annoyed; change the object as needed.

items.example: Her father loves blues records from the 1950s.
items.note: A genre with roots in African American musical traditions; mentioned in the R&B explanation.

items.example: I prefer pop music when I am exercising.
items.note: Pop appears in the unit's exercise advertisement.

items.example: She can read music even though she rarely performs.
items.note: To interpret written musical notation, not to read about music.

items.example: He can play by ear without looking at sheet music.
items.note: To perform what you hear without relying on written notation.

items.word: have a good ear for music
items.example: She has a good ear for music and notices tiny changes in pitch.
items.note: An informal way of describing a strong ability to hear and reproduce musical details.

items.example: After a few minutes, I could pick out a tune on the keyboard.
items.note: Informal: find and play the notes of a melody, often without formal training.

items.example: I recognised the tune immediately, but not the singer.
items.note: A melody, particularly one that can be sung or remembered.

items.example: Our neighbour is a talented musician who plays three instruments.
items.note: Talented means showing a natural or developed ability.

items.example: A trained musician helped the group prepare for the concert.
items.note: Someone who has received formal instruction in music.

items.example: You can make music with very simple instruments.
items.note: A broad collocation for producing or creating music.

items.example: She bought good headphones to enjoy music to the full.
items.note: To the full means as completely as possible; the core expression also works with other activities.

items.example: We heard wonderful music at the festival.
items.note: Music is normally uncountable: say some music, not some musics.

sectionsChecked: A: Downloading and managing your music
Common mistakes: classical music and uncountable music

units.title: Unit 22 — Food
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 50–51 (PDF pages 51–52).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Contrast common and nuanced words for flavour, including mild, savoury, sickly and moreish.
Describe food that is overcooked, undercooked, unripe, out of season or no longer fresh.
Discuss food quality, dietary preferences and a balanced diet with natural collocations.
Use restaurant vocabulary for bookings, courses and menus, plus polite expressions when hosting.

items.example: The sauce has a rich flavour without being too salty.
items.note: British spelling flavour, American flavor; the overall taste of food or drink.

items.example: The sauce is too hot for me to eat.
items.note: In this context hot refers to chilli heat, not temperature; compare spicy.

items.example: This spicy curry contains ginger and several chillies.
items.note: May describe noticeable spices and often chilli heat; not always the same as hot.

items.example: She ordered a mild curry rather than a very hot one.
items.note: For food, low in chilli heat or strong seasoning; opposite to hot or very spicy.

items.example: The soup was bland until I added some herbs.
items.note: Food with very little flavour; usually a negative assessment.

items.example: The roasted nuts were far too salty.
items.note: Containing a noticeable or excessive amount of salt.

items.example: That drink is too sugary for everyday use.
items.note: Containing a lot of sugar; often a negative description.

items.example: The icing was so sickly that nobody wanted another slice.
items.note: For sweet food, excessively rich or sugary in an unpleasant way.

items.example: We served savoury pastries before the main meal.
items.note: Usually describes food that is salty or seasoned rather than sweet; US spelling savory.

items.example: The yoghurt smelled fine but tasted unusually sour.
items.note: An acidic taste, such as lemon; may be pleasant or unpleasant depending on the food.

items.example: I enjoy bitter coffee without sugar.
items.note: A sharp taste associated with substances such as strong coffee.

items.example: The stew was simple but very tasty.
items.note: Pleasant in flavour; opposite to tasteless.

items.example: The vegetables were watery and tasteless.
items.note: Lacking flavour; also has a separate figurative meaning of offensive or vulgar.

items.pt: viciante de tão gostoso; dá vontade de comer mais
items.example: These roasted chickpeas are so moreish that I ate the whole bowl.
items.note: Informal British English: enjoyable enough that you want another portion.

items.example: I enjoy hot sauce; the hotter, the better.
items.note: Parallel comparative pattern: the more something increases, the more desirable it becomes.

items.section: B · Quality and condition of food
items.example: The pasta was overcooked and had become too soft.
items.note: Cooked for too long; often used for food that has lost its ideal texture.

items.section: B · Quality and condition of food
items.example: The steak was overdone for my taste.
items.note: Similar to overcooked, especially for meat and other prepared foods.

items.section: B · Quality and condition of food
items.example: The chicken was undercooked, so we returned it to the oven.
items.note: Not cooked enough; may also present a food-safety risk.

items.section: B · Quality and condition of food
items.example: The potatoes were underdone and still hard in the middle.
items.note: Similar to undercooked; not cooked sufficiently.

items.section: B · Quality and condition of food
items.example: The unripe pear was hard and rather sour.
items.note: For fruit or vegetables that have not matured enough to eat pleasantly.

items.section: B · Quality and condition of food
items.example: These peaches are ripe enough to eat today.
items.note: Ready to eat after maturing; opposite to unripe.

items.section: B · Quality and condition of food
items.example: Strawberries are cheaper when they are in season.
items.note: Being naturally harvested or readily available at a particular time of year.

items.section: B · Quality and condition of food
items.example: The milk may go off if it stays outside the fridge.
items.note: British English: become spoiled and no longer suitable to eat or drink.

items.section: B · Quality and condition of food
items.example: We had to throw out the yoghurt because it smelled bad.
items.note: Discard something; in British English, throw away is also common.

items.section: B · Quality and condition of food
items.example: I avoid heavy meals before going to bed.
items.note: Food that feels filling or difficult to digest, rather than high in physical weight.

items.section: B · Quality and condition of food
items.example: We ordered a light lunch before the afternoon walk.
items.note: Not too rich or filling; contrasts with heavy or stodgy food.

items.section: B · Quality and condition of food
items.example: The dumplings were rather stodgy, so I couldn't finish them.
items.note: British English for thick, filling food that is hard to digest; usually negative.

items.section: B · Quality and condition of food
items.example: They grow organic vegetables on a small farm.
items.note: Food produced according to organic production standards that restrict artificial inputs.

items.section: B · Quality and condition of food
items.example: She aims for a balanced diet with a variety of foods.
items.note: A pattern of eating with appropriate proportions of different nutrients and foods.

items.section: B · Quality and condition of food
items.example: He tries to eat less junk food during the working week.
items.note: Informal label for food generally considered high in salt, fat or sugar and low in nutritional value.

items.section: B · Quality and condition of food
items.example: We compared the labels on several processed foods.
items.note: Food altered or prepared before sale, often for convenience, preservation or flavour; processing levels vary.

items.example: We tend to eat out on Friday evenings.
items.note: Have a meal at a restaurant instead of at home.

items.example: We should book a table before the restaurant gets busy.
items.note: Common British English expression for reserving a restaurant table.

items.example: I called ahead to make a reservation for six people.
items.note: More formal alternative to book a table.

items.example: Let them know beforehand if you have an allergy.
items.note: Before the relevant event or time; often used with bookings and planning.

items.example: We had to cancel the booking because of the storm.
items.note: Natural collocation; booking is frequent in British English.

items.example: Please call to cancel a reservation if your plans change.
items.note: Alternative to cancel a booking, with the same restaurant meaning.

items.example: We ordered a three-course meal for the celebration.
items.note: One of the main stages in a meal, for example starter, main course and dessert.

items.example: We shared a starter before ordering our main dishes.
items.note: A small first course; also called an appetiser.

items.example: The chef prepared a light appetiser before dinner.
items.note: Another word for starter; US spelling appetizer.

items.example: The fish was served as the main course.
items.note: The largest or central course of a meal.

items.example: We decided to share a dessert after the meal.
items.note: A sweet course eaten after the main course; note the stress on the second syllable.

items.example: I ordered a side dish of grilled vegetables.
items.note: A smaller dish served alongside the main course.

items.example: The restaurant has a set menu at lunchtime.
items.note: A prearranged selection of dishes, often offered at a fixed price.

items.pt: à la carte; com pratos escolhidos individualmente
items.example: We ordered à la carte because everyone wanted something different.
items.note: Ordering separate dishes from a menu instead of a set menu; French-derived expression.

items.example: The day's specials were written on a board near the door.
items.note: Dishes offered for a limited period, often outside the regular menu.

items.pt: atender às necessidades de; oferecer opções para
items.example: The restaurant can cater for guests with different dietary needs.
items.note: British English: provide food or arrangements suitable for a group or requirement.

items.example: The menu offers three vegetarian main courses.
items.note: A person who does not eat meat or fish; also an adjective.

items.pt: pessoa que não come carne (mas pode comer peixe)
items.example: He's a non-meat-eater but sometimes orders fish.
items.note: The textbook contrasts this with vegetarian; here it can mean someone who avoids meat but eats fish.

items.example: My vegan colleague chose the vegetable curry.
items.note: Someone who avoids animal-derived foods and, generally, other animal products.

items.example: We asked the waiter for clean cutlery.
items.note: In British English, an uncountable collective noun for knives, forks and spoons.

items.example: She placed a napkin on her lap before eating.
items.note: A piece of cloth or paper used to keep clean during a meal.

items.example: Our host made everyone feel comfortable as they arrived.
items.note: The person who invites and looks after guests.

items.example: The rice was so good that several guests asked for seconds.
items.note: A second helping of food; usually used in the plural.

items.pt: sirva-se; fique à vontade para se servir
items.example: Please help yourself to some more bread.
items.note: Used to invite a guest to take food or drink without being served.

items.example: There is fruit and yoghurt for pudding.
items.note: Informal British English: pudding can mean dessert in general and is often uncountable in this use.

items.example: Would you like a sweet after dinner?
items.note: In British English, a sweet can mean dessert; sweet also means a small confection.

items.example: We saved some berries for afters.
items.note: Informal British English for dessert; used as a plural-looking noun.

items.example: May I refill your glass with water?
items.note: Refill means fill again; normally written as one word.

items.example: I'll pour the juice; just say when.
items.note: Conventional expression when offering to keep pouring until the other person says stop.

items.example: When! That's plenty, thank you.
items.note: The conventional response to say when; an everyday conversational use, not a time question.

items.example: We left some room for pudding after the roast.
items.note: An informal way to advise not eating too much before dessert.

sectionsChecked: A: Talking about flavours and tastes
B: Appearance, presentation and quality of food
